summary: Defines MIB objects for managing Ethernet-like interfaces, and it adds information useful for managing 10 gigabit per second Ethernet interfaces. It obsoletes RFC 2665. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This document defines the SNMP counters that describe an Ethernet port: how many frames had a bad checksum, how many collided, how many were too long. It updates the earlier version of the same MIB so that the counters also work on 10 gigabit links.

questions: what is the ethernet-like interface mib
which iftype should ethernet interfaces use
why do 10 gigabit ethernet interfaces need 64-bit counters
subtitle: The SNMP counters a manager reads to see how an Ethernet interface is behaving, updated for 10 gigabit links.

tldr.problem: Ethernet keeps getting faster and gaining new features, so the objects a manager reads to describe an Ethernet interface have to keep up. The previous version of this MIB had no counters that would not overflow on a fast link.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3635 keeps the dot3StatsTable of MAC layer error and collision counters and adds 64-bit versions of nine of them for high-speed links, plus two objects for the rate control function. It also spells out exactly how the Interfaces MIB counters relate to the IEEE 802.3 ones.
tldr.outcome: A manager can read per-interface error counters on 10 gigabit Ethernet without the counts wrapping. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2665 and is a Proposed Standard from September 2003 that has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 3635 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2003. It obsoletes RFC 2665, and it has not been obsoleted or updated since.

sections.title: A MIB That Keeps Up With Ethernet
sections.content:
This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base for use with network management protocols in the Internet community, and in particular defines objects for managing Ethernet-like interfaces. It also includes a MIB module that updates the list of managed objects specified in the earlier version of this module, RFC 2665, and it includes management information useful for the management of 10 Gigabit per second Ethernet interfaces.

Ethernet technology, as defined by the 802.3 Working Group of the IEEE, continues to evolve, with scalable increases in speed, new types of cabling and interfaces, and new features. This evolution may require changes in the managed objects in order to reflect this new functionality. This document reflects a certain stage in the evolution of Ethernet technology.

The definitions are based on Section 30, "10 Mb/s, 100 Mb/s, 1000 Mb/s and 10 Gb/s Management", and Annex 30A of IEEE Std 802.3, 2002 Edition, as amended by IEEE Std 802.3ae-2002. Implementors should note that the IEEE document explicitly describes, in the form of Pascal pseudocode, when, where and how various MAC attributes are measured, and it describes the effects of MAC actions that may be invoked by manipulating instances of the MIB objects defined here.
sections.plainLanguage: Ethernet gets faster and picks up new features, and the counters a manager reads have to change with it. This version of the Ethernet MIB adds what is needed for 10 gigabit links.

sections.title: What the Module Covers and What Changed
sections.content:
Instances of these object types represent attributes of an interface to an Ethernet-like communications medium. At present, Ethernet-like media are identified by the value ethernetCsmacd(6) of the ifType object in the Interfaces MIB, and some older implementations may return iso88023Csmacd(7) or starLan(11) for ifType for Ethernet-like media.

To the extent that some of the attributes defined in the IEEE standard are represented by previously defined objects in MIB-2 or in the Interfaces MIB, such attributes are not redundantly represented by objects defined in this memo. Among the attributes represented by objects defined in other memos are the number of octets transmitted or received on a particular interface, the number of frames transmitted or received on a particular interface, the promiscuous status of an interface, the MAC address of an interface, and multicast information associated with an interface.

What this module adds is the MAC layer detail: the dot3StatsTable holds one row for each Ethernet-like interface in the system, indexed by dot3StatsIndex, whose value identifies the same interface as the same value of ifIndex. The columns are the error and collision counters of the MAC layer: alignment errors, FCS errors, single collision frames, multiple collision frames, SQE test errors, deferred transmissions, late collisions, excessive collisions, internal MAC transmit errors, carrier sense errors, frame too longs, internal MAC receive errors, symbol errors, the duplex status, and the rate control ability and status.

The change log enumerates the changes made to RFC 2665 to produce this document. The references to the IEEE 802.3 standard were updated to refer to the 2002 edition, and a reference to IEEE 802.3ae-2002 was added. The DESCRIPTION clauses for dot3StatsAlignmentErrors and dot3StatsSymbolErrors were updated to reflect behaviour on 10 Gb/s interfaces.

Two objects were added for management of the rate control function in WAN applications of Ethernet: dot3StatsRateControlAbility and dot3StatsRateControlStatus. Nine 64-bit counters were added to support operation on high-speed Ethernet interfaces: dot3HCControlInUnknownOpcodes, dot3HCInPauseFrames, dot3HCOutPauseFrames, dot3HCStatsAlignmentErrors, dot3HCStatsFCSErrors, dot3HCStatsFrameTooLongs, dot3HCStatsInternalMacTransmitErrors, dot3HCStatsInternalMacReceiveErrors and dot3HCStatsSymbolErrors. Object groups and compliances were added to contain the new objects, and the MODULE-IDENTITY clause was updated to reflect the changes in the MIB module.

The use of the various ifType values for Ethernet was clarified to emphasize that all Ethernet-like interfaces must use the ethernetCsmacd ifType, and several clarifications were made to the section on the mapping of the Interface MIB objects to Ethernet.
sections.plainLanguage:
The general counters about a port live in the Interfaces MIB. This module supplies the ones that only make sense for Ethernet: checksum failures, collisions, frames that were too long, and the duplex setting.

The previous version of this MIB had no counters that would not wrap on a fast link, so this version adds nine 64-bit counters and two objects for the rate control function.

sections.title: Which Interface Type to Report
sections.content:
This MIB applies to interfaces which have the ifType value ethernetCsmacd(6). It is REQUIRED that all Ethernet-like interfaces use an ifType of ethernetCsmacd(6) regardless of the speed that the interface is running or the link-layer encapsulation in use. Use of the ifType values iso88023Csmacd(7) and starLan(11) is deprecated, although some older implementations may return these values, and management applications should be prepared to receive them.

Three other interface types defined in the IANAifType-MIB for Ethernet are fastEther(62), fastEtherFX(69) and gigabitEthernet(117). These were registered by individual vendors, not by any IETF working group. A requirement for compliance is that all Ethernet-like interfaces MUST return ethernetCsmacd(6) for ifType and MUST NOT return fastEther(62), fastEtherFX(69) or gigabitEthernet(117), but management applications SHOULD be prepared to receive them from older implementations. Information on the particular flavour of Ethernet that an interface is running is available from ifSpeed in the Interfaces MIB and ifMauType in the 802.3 MAU MIB.

Speed reporting follows the same idea. For interfaces operating at 1000 Mb/s or less, ifSpeed gives the operational speed in bits per second, and ifHighSpeed gives it in millions of bits per second: 1, 10, 100 or 1,000. For interfaces operating at greater than 1000 Mb/s, ifHighSpeed gives the operational speed in millions of bits per second, equal to 10,000 for LAN implementations of 10 Gb/s and 9,294 for WAN implementations of the 10 Gb/s MAC over an OC-192 PHY. For these speeds ifSpeed should report the maximum unsigned 32-bit value of 4,294,967,295. These objects MUST NOT indicate a doubled value when operating in full-duplex mode.
sections.plainLanguage: Every Ethernet port, whatever its speed, must report the same interface type. The speed is reported separately, and above 1 gigabit the 32-bit speed field simply reports its maximum, with the real figure in the high-speed field.

sections.title: How the Counters Relate to the IEEE Ones
sections.content:
The Interfaces MIB octet counters, ifInOctets, ifOutOctets, ifHCInOctets and ifHCOutOctets, MUST include all octets in valid frames sent or received on the interface, including the MAC header and FCS, but not the preamble, start of frame delimiter or extension octets. They do not include the number of octets in collided or failed transmit attempts, since the MAC layer driver typically has no visibility to count them, and they do not include octets in received invalid frames, since that information is normally not passed to the MAC layer.

The IF-MIB counters do not exactly match the IEEE 802.3 octet counters. The IEEE counters aOctetsTransmittedOK and aOctetsReceivedOK count only the octets in the clientData and Pad fields, whereas ifInOctets and ifOutOctets include the entire MAC frame. The IF-MIB counters can be derived from the IEEE 802.3 counters as follows: ifInOctets equals aOctetsReceivedOK plus 18 times aFramesReceivedOK, and ifOutOctets equals aOctetsTransmittedOK plus 18 times aFramesTransmittedOK.

The packet counters differ in the same way. The IEEE frame counters count frames actually sent or received, while the IF-MIB counters count requests made by a higher layer, whether or not the attempt succeeded. Roughly, aFramesTransmittedOK equals the sum of the unicast, multicast and broadcast output counters plus the output pause frames, minus ifOutErrors and ifOutDiscards. Similarly, aFramesReceivedOK equals the sum of the unicast, multicast and broadcast input counters plus the input pause frames, plus ifInDiscards and ifInUnknownProtos.

This specification chooses to treat MAC control frames as being originated and consumed within the interface and not counted by the IF-MIB packet counters. MAC control frames are normally sent as multicast packets, and in many environments they can greatly outnumber multicast frames carrying actual data, so including them would render the multicast counters considerably less useful.
sections.plainLanguage: The counters in the Interfaces MIB and the ones in the IEEE standard count slightly different things. The RFC gives the formulas to convert between them, so a manager can compare numbers from either source.

sections.title: Addresses on the Interface
sections.content:
The ifPhysAddress object contains the IEEE 802.3 address which is placed in the source-address field of any Ethernet, Starlan or IEEE 802.3 frames that originate at this interface. Usually this will be kept in ROM on the interface hardware, though some systems may set it via software. Where a system has several such addresses, the address chosen should be the one most likely to be of use to network management, such as the address placed in ARP responses for systems which are primarily IP systems. If the designer truly cannot choose, the factory-provided ROM address is suggested, and if the address cannot be determined an octet string of zero length should be returned. The address is stored in binary in canonical bit order, that is, the Group Bit is positioned as the low-order bit of the first octet, so the first byte of a multicast address has the bit 0x01 set.

The ifRcvAddressTable contains all IEEE 802.3 addresses, unicast, multicast and broadcast, for which this interface will receive packets and forward them up to a higher layer entity for local consumption, and the format of the address is the same as for ifPhysAddress. In the event that the interface is part of a MAC bridge, this table does not include unicast addresses accepted for possible forwarding out of another port, and the table is explicitly not intended to provide a bridge address filtering mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Two objects describe addresses: the hardware address of the port, and the table of addresses the port will accept packets for.

sections.title: Neighbouring MIBs and Deprecated Objects
sections.content:
Support for the mauModIfCompl3 compliance statement of the MAU-MIB is REQUIRED for Ethernet-like interfaces. That MIB is needed so applications can determine the current MAU type in use by the interface and control autonegotiation and duplex mode. Implementing this MIB module without implementing the MAU-MIB would leave applications with no standard way to determine the media type in use, and no standard way to control the duplex mode of the interface.

This document defines an object called dot3StatsEtherChipSet, used to identify the MAC hardware used to communicate on an interface. Previous versions of this document contained a number of OID assignments for existing Ethernet chipsets, and maintaining that list as part of the document proved to be problematic, so those assignments have been moved to a separate document. The object has now been deprecated. Implementation feedback indicates that the object is much more useful in theory than in practice, and its utility in debugging network problems in the field appears to be limited; where it may be useful it is not sufficient, since it identifies only the MAC chip and not the PHY, PMD or driver. The administrative overhead of maintaining a central registry of chipset OIDs cannot be justified for an object whose usefulness is questionable at best.

The RFC also maps the IEEE 802.3 managed objects to their SNMP counterparts, so a manager that knows the IEEE names can find the SNMP ones: aFrameCheckSequenceErrors corresponds to dot3StatsFCSErrors, aAlignmentErrors to dot3StatsAlignmentErrors, aLateCollisions to dot3StatsLateCollisions, aDuplexStatus to dot3StatsDuplexStatus, aCollisionFrames to dot3CollFrequencies, and aPromiscuousStatus to ifPromiscuousMode in the Interfaces MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: Two more things are settled here: the MAU MIB is required so a manager can see the duplex setting, and the object that named the Ethernet chip is dropped because it was not useful in practice.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
There is one management object defined in this MIB that has a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write: dot3PauseAdminMode. It may be used to change the flow control configuration on a network interface, which may result in dropped packets, or in sending flow control packets on links where the link partner will not understand them. Either action could be detrimental to network performance.

Some of the readable objects may also be considered sensitive. In particular, dot3StatsEtherChipSet may be considered sensitive in many environments, since it would allow an intruder to obtain information about which vendor's equipment is in use on the network, although that object has been deprecated. Most of the objects in this MIB module contain statistical information about particular network links, which in some environments may be considered sensitive, so it is important to control even GET and NOTIFY access to them and possibly to encrypt the values when sending them over the network via SNMP.

SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and even if the network itself is secure there is no control over who on that network may GET or SET the objects in this MIB. It is recommended that implementors consider the security features provided by the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for its cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy, and that deployment of SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: Only one object here can be written, and writing it changes the flow control on the port, which could hurt the link. The counters reveal what the port is doing, so they should be protected too.

items.title: Alignment errors
items.text: Frames received whose bits did not align to the octet boundary.

items.title: FCS errors
items.text: Frames received with a bad frame check sequence.

items.title: Single collision frames
items.text: Frames that collided once before being sent.

items.title: Multiple collision frames
items.text: Frames that collided more than once.

items.title: Late collisions
items.text: A collision seen after the frame should have been sent.

items.title: Excessive collisions
items.text: Frames abandoned because of too many collisions.

items.title: Frame too longs
items.text: Received frames longer than the interface allows.

items.title: Symbol errors
items.text: Bad symbols on the physical layer, added for 10 Gb/s.

data.title: IF-MIB octet counters from the IEEE 802.3 ones
data.code:
ifInOctets  = aOctetsReceivedOK + (18 * aFramesReceivedOK)
ifOutOctets = aOctetsTransmittedOK + (18 * aFramesTransmittedOK)
